comparison: Frozen R2 versus R3, four direct English chapter summaries

followup_scaffold_validation.ruff: passed for changed taskset and existing tests

interpretation: R3 shows partial content gains on three readable comparisons, alongside persistent factual errors, poor compression and a format regression on Bennett. This is not an aggregate capability win or a reliable summarization system.

One sampled episode per model/chapter, fresh native sessions and one errored R3 episode limit causal and generalization claims. Evening-access was prospective after the R3 data freeze and is now development-exposed; none of these four sources is admitted to TRAIN.

Matched task identities and model-visible source hashes were verified across arms. Existing readable exports exactly match their trace.info artifacts. Source hashes here include runtime paragraph-ID annotations; they differ from raw chapter-file hashes.

The native end_turn on R3 evening-access proves the agent stopped, not that the artifact met the task. The R2 Bennett reward certifies structural format only and coexists with a reversed central argument.

R3 city-shade's 541.952-second agent duration and EOF closely match the configured 540-second GNU timeout plus cleanup. Timeout is a strong inference, not directly verified by an exit-code receipt. Its last intercepted call has ClientConnectionResetError; no ProviderError is recorded.

The city-shade trace shows the model describing a successful write as failed after generic file-write recovery feedback. The scaffold incorrectly conflates repeated successful calls with Python errors. A task-local feedback fix is prepared separately; this comparison used the older scaffold.
R4 already continues from R3 with 44 episodes and 64 dense updates. This review guides subsequent learning and does not impose a pass threshold for further weight updates.
next_actions: Evaluate R4 against frozen R3 on matched harness/scaffold settings after R4 finishes and the host drains. Any scaffold change must apply equally to both arms and be labeled.

Train further on source-grounded compression, numerical units, chapter boundaries, qualifications, and responding to format corrections using TRAIN-only material. Keep known erroneous suffixes out of successful imitation targets.
Keep semantic assessment separate from format scores and reduce repetitive file-write coaching; no automatic summary rewriting by the scaffold.

episodes.label: r2-vs-r3-direct-four-chapters-r1-baseline-direct-alice-ch1
episodes.summary: Alice is bored sitting by her sister on the bank, considering a daisy-chain but deciding against it. A White Rabbit with pink eyes runs past her, takes a watch, and hurries off. Alice follows the rabbit through a rabbit-hole under the hedge, falling down a tunnel into a deep well filled with cupboards and bookshelves. The fall ends when she hits a heap of sticks and leaves, emerging in a long, low hall with locked doors. She finds a three-legged glass table with a golden key, opens a small door behind a curtain, and enters a small garden with bright flowers and cool fountains. She drinks a bottle labeled "DRINK ME," shrinks to ten inches tall, and wanders the garden.
episodes.semantic_review: Unmarked prose incorrectly says Alice enters and wanders the garden. It omits the unreachable key and cake ending. The chapter ends with her finishing the cake, before any garden entry.

episodes.label: r2-vs-r3-direct-four-chapters-r1-baseline-direct-bennett-ch1
episodes.summary:
* Time is the real wealth with an unlimited supply, unlike money which is scarce and encumbers the earth.
* People waste time through poor management rather than lack of it, as shown by the man who has enough income but not enough time.
* Happiness depends entirely on how well time is spent, not on accumulating more money.
* Once you realize you have all the time in the world, you stop wasting it and begin to manage it effectively.
episodes.semantic_review: Four structurally valid bullets reverse the central argument: the source says time is a restricted 24-hour daily allowance and money is common, not unlimited time and scarce money. The opening money-management example is misread, and automatic improvement after realization is unsupported.

episodes.label: r2-vs-r3-direct-four-chapters-r1-baseline-direct-city-shade
episodes.summary:
Summer heat study in Bellwick compared twelve streets with and without mature trees.
Shaded streets were cooler on average, but the difference was largest late afternoon.
This does not establish how much planting immediately cools a neighborhood.
Shade reduces pavement and people's heat absorption.
Trees release water vapor that cools air.
episodes.semantic_review: Five unmarked lines cover only the initial comparison and mechanisms. 'Twelve streets with and without' obscures twelve per group; route-level access, maintenance, temporary shade, species risk and study limitations are omitted.

episodes.label: r2-vs-r3-direct-four-chapters-r1-baseline-direct-evening-access
episodes.summary: The trial showed evening access increased weekly visits by 14% but lowered the average hourly rate. The extra visits came from existing users, not new residents. The trial was temporary with no permanent funding secured. The recommendation is to run a narrower test on one evening before deciding.
episodes.semantic_review: Unmarked prose preserves higher weekly visits and a lower hourly rate, but falsely asserts additional visits came from existing users. The source cannot distinguish users. It omits step-free access as a prerequisite and confounding/measurement limits.

episodes.label: r2-vs-r3-direct-four-chapters-r1-candidate-direct-alice-ch1
episodes.summary:
Alice was tired of sitting by her sister on the bank, so she considered whether making a daisy-chain was worth getting up and picking the daisies. A White Rabbit with pink eyes ran close by, took a watch, and hurried on. Alice followed, running across the field after it and falling down a rabbit-hole under the hedge.
The rabbit-hole went straight on like a tunnel, then dipped down into a deep well. Alice looked around but could not see what she was coming to; the well was filled with cupboards and book-shelves. She took down a jar of orange marmalade but it was empty.
Down, down, down. Alice wondered how many miles she had fallen by and whether she would fall through the earth. She thought she might be near the Antipathies and asked what country she was in, but there was no one listening.
After twenty-four thousand miles down, Alice found a heap of sticks and dry leaves where the fall was over. She jumped up on her feet, found the White Rabbit still hurrying down a low, lamp-lit hall, and was just in time to hear it say, 'How late it’s getting!' The Rabbit was no longer to be seen.
There were doors all round the hall, but they were all locked. Alice walked sadly down the middle, wondering how she was ever to get out again. She came upon a little three-legged table with a tiny golden key, then a low curtain and a little door about fifteen inches high. She opened the door and found a small passage into a lovely garden.
She went back to the table and found a small bottle with the words 'DRINK ME' on it. Alice did not want to do that in a hurry; she first looked to see whether it was marked 'poison'. The bottle was not marked 'poison', so she tasted it and found it very nice. She very soon finished it off.
'A curious feeling!' said Alice; 'I must be shutting up like a telescope.' She was now only ten inches high and her face brightened at the thought that she was now the right size for going through the little door into the garden. She waited a few minutes to see if she was going to shrink any further, but when she got to the door she found she had forgotten the little golden key.
She went back to the table for it, but could not possibly reach it. She could see it through the glass, so she tried her best to climb up one of the legs of the table but it was too slippery. The poor little thing sat down and cried.
'So many out-of-the-way things have happened lately!' thought Alice, 'that I have begun to think that very few things indeed are really impossible.' She went to the little glass box lying under the table and found in it a very small cake with the words 'EAT ME' on it.
She ate a little bit and said anxiously, 'Which way?'. She held her hand on the top of her head to feel which way it was growing, but was surprised to find that she remained the same size. So she set to work and very soon finished off the cake.
episodes.semantic_review: Partial chronology improvement: empty jar, shrink before unreachable key, cake initially unchanged and then finished; no claim of garden entry. But a twenty-four-thousand-mile fall is invented and the 547-word, ten-paragraph retelling is not a key-bullet summary.

episodes.label: r2-vs-r3-direct-four-chapters-r1-candidate-direct-bennett-ch1
episodes.summary:
Chapter 1 argues that time is the most precious possession, unlike money, which can be hoarded and spent. Time cannot be stolen or given away, and no one receives more or less than one receives. In an ideal democracy, there is no aristocracy of wealth or intellect; genius is never rewarded by an extra hour a day, and there is no punishment for waste. The supply of time is truly a daily miracle, and one cannot get into debt because one cannot waste to-morrow.

The chapter observes that many people do not manage their time effectively. They waste money, forget the quality of food, or fail to balance their daily life. People feel an uneasy certainty that their fine suit is not surmounted by a shameful hat or that they have forgotten the quality of the food.

The author concludes that they have always had all the time there is, and the realization of this truth has led to a minute practical examination of daily time-expenditure.
episodes.semantic_review: Partial argument improvement: equal allocation, no borrowing from tomorrow, and all available time are retained without the unlimited-time/scarce-money reversal. Explicit 24 hours is omitted; suit/food analogies are misread and uneasy feeling becomes uneasy certainty. Three prose paragraphs fail the requested format.

episodes.label: r2-vs-r3-direct-four-chapters-r1-candidate-direct-evening-access
episodes.summary: The trial found that evening access increased weekly visits by 14 per cent but lowered the average hourly rate. Evening opening requires a separate agreement with the building operator and cost estimate, neither of which was secured. The trial coincided with an examination period and new adult education class, so no comparison site exists. A temporary grant covered 1,920 staff hours but ended with the trial; no permanent funding was committed. The side entrance was not recorded as step-free, and two respondents reported being unable to use it. The review group recommended a conditional twelve-week test on one evening a week, pending replacement funding and a reliable step-free entrance. The trial demonstrated evening opening could be delivered under temporary arrangements but did not settle which continuing arrangement should be adopted.
episodes.semantic_review: Partial coverage improvement: temporary funding, accessibility prerequisites and the conditional one-evening test are retained; the definite existing-users claim is absent. But 1,920 staffing cost becomes 1,920 staff hours (actual 96 hours), the building agreement is generalized from the step-free entrance to evening opening, and independent confounds/no-comparison facts are conflated. Native end_turn with one unmarked paragraph, not compliant bullets.
